title: “IF WE SAY WE HAVE NO SIN…” — THE TERRIFYING WARNING WE KEEP SKIPPING BEFORE AND AFTER 1 JOHN 1:9
paragraphs: “IF WE SAY WE HAVE NO SIN…” — THE TERRIFYING WARNING WE KEEP SKIPPING BEFORE AND AFTER 1 JOHN 1:9

We love the promise that God will forgive us. But what happens when we want His forgiveness without admitting what needs to be forgiven? The verses surrounding one of Christianity’s most comforting promises expose a dangerous kind of spiritual blindness—and reveal why the blood of Jesus is still our only hope.
There is something deeply unsettling about a person who can kneel before God, sing about the blood of Jesus, lift their hands during worship, quote Scripture with confidence…
And still refuse to admit they are wrong.
Not because they have never sinned.
Not because they have reached perfection.
But because somewhere along the way, they learned how to defend what God was calling them to confess.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that they can do it while genuinely believing they are close to Him.
Read that again.
Because there is a kind of spiritual danger that does not begin when someone openly rejects Jesus.
Sometimes it begins when someone becomes so comfortable talking about Jesus that they stop allowing His truth to confront them.
They know the language of grace.
They know the promises of forgiveness.
They know how to say, “Nobody is perfect.”
But when the Holy Spirit brings a particular sin into the light, suddenly there is an explanation.
A justification.
Someone else to blame.
A painful history to point toward.
A circumstance that supposedly makes disobedience understandable.
And before long, confession has been replaced by self-defense.
This is why the apostle John wrote something that should make every professing Christian examine their heart.
Not merely the obvious sinner.
Not merely the person who walked away from church.
Not merely the believer struggling with an addiction, an angry temper, a secret habit, or a compromised relationship.
Every one of us.
Because the warning surrounding 1 John 1:9 was never written to entertain our curiosity about other people's sins.
It was written to confront what happens when we refuse to acknowledge our own.
And if you have ever whispered, “Lord, forgive me,” while secretly hoping He would not touch a particular area of your life, what follows may feel painfully familiar.
John writes:
Notice what John does not say.
He does not say that the person has stopped using religious language.
He does not say the person has abandoned every outward appearance of Christianity.
He says someone can claim fellowship with God while walking in darkness.
That is the danger.
A profession of faith can become disconnected from a life that is being brought under the truth of Christ.
A person may know how to appear spiritually healthy while hiding what is spiritually destructive.
They may speak tenderly about forgiveness while refusing to forgive.
They may condemn dishonesty while protecting their own deception.
They may publicly celebrate holiness while privately making peace with what Scripture condemns.
They may share verses about love while quietly nurturing hatred.
And the longer they avoid the light, the more normal the darkness begins to feel.
Until conviction feels like condemnation.
Correction feels like persecution.
And anyone who lovingly confronts them becomes an enemy.
But John is not finished.
He continues:
“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — 1 John 1:7, KJV
Do not miss the breathtaking beauty of that sentence.
John does not say that walking in the light means we have become people who no longer need cleansing.
He says that those walking in the light are cleansed by the blood of Jesus.
The light is not the reward for people who have successfully hidden every flaw.
It is where sinners come because they need the Savior.
Walking in the light is not a performance of sinless perfection. It is a life oriented toward God's revealed truth, where sin is no longer defended as though it belongs on the throne.
And then John delivers the warning that gives this entire passage its piercing force.
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” — 1 John 1:8, KJV
We deceive ourselves.
Not merely other people.
Ourselves.
There is something more dangerous than being exposed by the truth.
It is becoming convinced that the truth has nothing left to expose.
Consider the original Greek.
John writes:
ἐὰν εἴπωμεν ὅτι ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἔχομεν, ἑαυτοὺς πλανῶμεν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἡμῖν.
A close translation is:
“If we say that we do not have sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
The phrase ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἔχομεν (hamartian ouk echomen) means “we do not have sin.”
John is addressing the claim that sin is absent from us.
And the verb πλανῶμεν (planōmen) means “we deceive” or “we lead astray.”
Here it describes self-deception.
This matters because John is not simply criticizing people who commit sins.
He is exposing the falsehood of claiming to have no sin.
He is confronting the kind of spiritual self-understanding that makes confession seem unnecessary.
Think about that.
The person who admits, “I am struggling, and I need Jesus,” may be painfully aware of their weakness.
But the person who insists, “There is nothing wrong with me,” may be shutting the door against the very truth that could bring them to repentance.
One is wounded and reaching for the Physician.
The other is insisting there is no wound.
And that brings us to the verse so many believers love to quote.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Beautiful.
Glorious.
Life-giving.
But it is not an isolated religious slogan.
It stands between two warnings against denying sin.
Before the promise, John says that claiming to have no sin is self-deception.
After the promise, he says something even more sobering.
“If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.” — 1 John 1:10, KJV
Do you see the progression?
In verse 8, denying sin deceives ourselves.
In verse 10, claiming we have not sinned contradicts God's testimony and effectively makes Him out to be a liar.
And between those warnings stands the mercy of God.
Confession.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
It is as though John is showing us two radically different responses to the truth.
We can deny our sin.
Or we can confess it.
We can protect our self-image.
Or we can come honestly before the Savior.
We can insist that we need no cleansing.
Or we can trust the One whose blood cleanses from all sin.
And there is something profoundly beautiful about the Greek word translated “confess.”
ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen.
It comes from the verb ὁμολογέω (homologeō), which carries the sense of acknowledging, admitting, or confessing.
In this context, confession means truthfully acknowledging our sins before God rather than denying them.
It is not a magic word.
It is not a formula that forces God to respond.
It is not a performance designed to convince Him that we have suffered enough.
It is coming into agreement with the truth about what we have done.
No disguise.
No courtroom speech.
No carefully constructed defense.
Just the truth.
“Lord, I sinned.”
Not, “Lord, I made a mistake, but You know what they did to me.”
Not, “Lord, technically I was wrong, but my intentions were good.”
Not, “Lord, everyone does it.”
Not, “Lord, at least I am not as bad as someone else.”
Just…
“Father, I have sinned against You.”
And suddenly, something changes.
Not because confession earns the cross.
Not because tears purchase forgiveness.
Not because shame has finally become intense enough to satisfy divine justice.
But because the person has stopped pretending and is turning toward the mercy God provides in Jesus Christ.
That is where grace becomes more than a beautiful word on a Christian shirt.
It becomes the only hope of a guilty heart.
Maybe you know what this feels like.
Maybe there was a moment when you knew exactly what God was confronting.
A message you should not have sent.
A conversation you should not have entertained.
A lie that became easier to repeat.
A bitterness you kept feeding.
A habit you kept promising to surrender.
A relationship where you were more concerned about winning than loving.
A private compromise nobody at church could see.
And for a while, you managed to keep going.
You still prayed.
Still attended services.
Still listened to worship music.
Still posted encouraging Scriptures.
But whenever the truth came too close, you quickly moved away from it.
You told yourself you would deal with it later.
When life became less stressful.
When the temptation became weaker.
When the other person apologized.
When you felt spiritually stronger.
When you were finally ready.
But the days became weeks.
The weeks became months.
And the sin you once trembled over became something you barely questioned.
That is why this passage is not merely theological information.
It is a merciful alarm.
Because sin rarely announces, “I am here to destroy your fellowship with God.”
Sometimes it whispers, “You deserve this.”
Sometimes, “It is not that serious.”
Sometimes, “God understands.”
And yes, God understands our weakness far more deeply than we do.
But His understanding is not permission to call darkness light.
His compassion is not indifference toward the things that wound us and others.
His grace is not an invitation to protect the very sin from which Christ came to save us.
Paul confronts that misunderstanding in Romans 6:1–2, asking whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may increase.
His answer is emphatic: God forbid.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace brings us to the Savior who forgives and transforms.
And perhaps someone reading this has misunderstood repentance for years.
You thought repentance meant becoming worthy enough for God to receive you.
You thought you had to clean yourself up before you could pray.
You thought you needed to prove that this time would be different before approaching Jesus again.
So every failure pushed you further into hiding.
Every relapse into an old pattern made you feel disqualified.
Every memory of your past whispered that your testimony had been ruined.
But listen carefully.
John did not write, “If we confess our sins, God might forgive us if our spiritual record has improved enough.”
He wrote:
“He is faithful and just to forgive us.”
Faithful.
And just.
That second word matters.
The Greek is δίκαιος — dikaios, meaning righteous or just.
God's forgiveness is not moral carelessness.
He does not pretend evil never happened.
He does not dismiss wrongdoing as though holiness were unimportant.
The foundation of Christian forgiveness is the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And John immediately directs us there.
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” — 1 John 2:1, KJV
There it is.
The heart of the Gospel.
John's purpose is not to encourage sin.
He explicitly writes so that his readers will not sin.
Yet he also knows that believers need to hear where their hope rests when they do.
Jesus Christ the righteous.
Our Advocate.
The Greek word is παράκλητον — paraklēton, from παράκλητος (paraklētos), a term used for someone called alongside to help, advocate, or intercede.
And John does not leave us with an abstract picture of someone speaking kind words about us.
He identifies Jesus as the righteous One.
Then he continues:
“And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.” — 1 John 2:2, KJV
The Greek word translated “propitiation” is ἱλασμός — hilasmos.
It refers here to Christ's atoning sacrifice, through which the problem of human sin before a holy God is decisively addressed.
Christian traditions differ in how they explain every aspect of the term, particularly its relationship to divine wrath and the removal of sin. But the central truth of the passage is unmistakable.
Our forgiveness rests on Jesus and His sacrificial work, not on our ability to manufacture innocence.
The One who calls us to confess is the One who has provided the Savior.
This is why the Christian life cannot be reduced to either of two destructive extremes.
One says, “My sin does not matter because God is gracious.”
The other says, “My sin is too great for God's grace.”
Both fail to see the cross clearly.
The cross tells us that sin is serious enough to require the death of the Son of God.
And that God's love is great enough that the Son willingly gave Himself for sinners.
You cannot look at Calvary and honestly call sin harmless.
But neither can you look at the crucified and risen Christ and conclude that a repentant sinner must remain beyond the reach of His mercy.
Think of Peter.
He was not a stranger to Jesus.
He had walked with Him.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed His miracles.
He had declared his loyalty with confidence.
And then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denial.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
Peter denied knowing the very Lord he had promised never to abandon.
Luke 22:61–62 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered Jesus' words.
Then he went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine the weight of that moment.
The voice that once declared loyalty had spoken denial.
The courage he believed he possessed had collapsed.
And suddenly, Peter could no longer hide behind his confidence.
His failure was real.
His tears were real.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21:15–19, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Jesus did not treat denial as something harmless.
Nor did He abandon Peter as though his failure had made restoration impossible.
The man who had publicly denied Jesus was graciously restored and called to serve.
That is not permission to sin.
That is the wonder of grace.
And perhaps this is the part of the story you need to hear.
Your past may be scandalous.
Your choices may have caused real damage.
You may need to apologize, make restitution where possible, accept consequences, seek accountability, and rebuild trust slowly.
Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence.
Repentance does not entitle you to immediate reconciliation with someone you have harmed.
And grace must never be used to pressure an injured person to ignore abuse, abandon boundaries, or pretend that everything is safe.
But even when the consequences remain, the Gospel announces that sin does not have to be your master and shame does not have to be your identity.
In Christ, there is forgiveness.
In Christ, there is a new way to walk.
In Christ, there is hope for genuine transformation.
From scandal to grace does not mean the scandal never happened. It means the scandal does not get the final word when Jesus redeems a life.
And now we need to confront another uncomfortable truth.
Some people confess sin with their lips while continuing to defend it in their hearts.
They say, “Forgive me,” but have already decided to return to the same wrongdoing without resistance.
They want relief from guilt without surrendering the behavior.
They want peace with God while refusing to listen to His Word.
But biblical confession is not meant to become a ritual that protects unrepentance.
Proverbs 28:13 teaches that the person who conceals transgressions will not prosper, while the one who confesses and forsakes them obtains mercy.
Notice both movements.
Confession.
And forsaking.
This does not mean genuine repentance guarantees that a believer will never struggle or fall again.
Spiritual growth can involve difficult battles, painful setbacks, and the ongoing need for God's grace.
But there is a difference between fighting sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and declaring that the fall no longer matters.
There is a difference between a wounded conscience crying for mercy and a hardened heart insisting it needs none.
John's warning should make us examine that difference honestly.
And if your conscience is tender right now, please do not misunderstand what you are reading.
This article is not telling the believer who hates their sin and longs for holiness that every struggle proves they are a fraud.
Nor is it asking you to spend your life obsessively searching for hidden wrongdoing until you lose sight of Jesus.
John's letter offers assurance as well as warning.
He wants believers to know the truth, reject darkness, love one another, and find confidence in the Son of God.
The goal of confession is not endless self-condemnation.
The goal is restored honesty before God and a life increasingly shaped by His truth.
There is a difference between the conviction that leads us toward Christ and the despair that tells us to run away from Him.
The Gospel calls us toward Christ.
Always toward Christ.
When David was confronted about his sin, he could no longer preserve the illusion of innocence.
His wrongdoing involved adultery, deception, and the arranged death of Uriah, as recorded in 2 Samuel 11–12.
The consequences were grievous.
And when the prophet Nathan confronted him, David said, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV).
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a heart that no longer wants to hide.
In verse 17, David speaks of a broken and contrite heart that God will not despise.
Not a heart proud of its religious reputation.
Not a heart bargaining for a better public image.
A contrite heart.
A heart that knows the truth.
And this brings us back to 1 John.
Because the most dangerous words in the passage may not be spoken by someone openly rebelling against God.
They may be spoken by someone who has become too confident in their own spiritual condition to hear correction.
“I have no sin.”
“I have done nothing wrong.”
“I do not need to repent.”
But the safest place for a sinner is not behind a convincing defense.
It is before the Savior who already knows the truth.
You do not need to surprise God with your confession.
You cannot tell Him something He has not already seen.
He knows the thoughts you would never post.
The jealousy you never admitted.
The anger you disguised as righteousness.
The pride you called discernment.
The resentment you called wisdom.
The selfishness you called self-protection.
The fear you covered with religious activity.
And still, the Gospel calls you to come to Jesus.
Not to celebrate the darkness.
Not to excuse it.
But to leave it behind and walk in His light.
Maybe your most important prayer tonight is not a long, impressive prayer.
Maybe it is five honest words.
“Lord Jesus, I have sinned.”
And then…
“Please forgive me. Change me.”
There is no shame in needing the Savior.
The tragedy is refusing Him because we insist we have nothing from which we need to be saved.
And to the person who has been away from God for a long time, hear this clearly.
You are not being invited to join a community of people who have never failed.
You are being invited to turn to the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
The One who bore sin.
The One who conquered death.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The One who makes forgiveness and new life possible.
If you have never entrusted yourself to Christ, do not settle for admiring His teachings from a distance.
Come to Him in faith.
Turn from sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Ask Him for mercy.
And begin learning what it means to follow Him.
If you already belong to Him but have been hiding, stop treating His light as though it were your enemy.
The light that exposes sin also reveals the Savior.
And if this truth has uncovered something you have been avoiding, I want to invite you into a moment of genuine honesty.
You do not need to reveal private details or confess sensitive matters to strangers on the internet.
Not as a public performance.
Not to prove your salvation.
But as a small, honest acknowledgment that you still need the grace of God.
Someone else may be quietly wondering whether change is possible.
Your words might help them look to Christ rather than surrender to despair.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who needs to read this.
Not because you have decided they are worse than you.
Not because you want to expose them.
But because they may be carrying a burden you cannot see.
A father ashamed of his anger.
A mother overwhelmed by guilt.
A young believer trapped in secrecy.
A church member exhausted from maintaining appearances.
A friend who thinks one terrible chapter has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Sometimes a private message is the more loving choice.

Not because every sentence needs to be remembered, but because the next time shame tells you to hide—or pride tells you that you have nothing to confess—you may need to return to the words of 1 John 1:5–2:2.
Read the whole passage.
Read what comes before the promise.
Read what comes after it.
And remember that the same apostle who warned against denying sin also pointed directly to Jesus Christ the righteous, our Advocate with the Father.
This is the kind of biblical truth we want to keep sharing through Gospel Warrior.
Not a faith built on emotional excitement alone.
Not messages that flatter us while leaving our hearts untouched.
But Scripture that helps us understand the Gospel, confront sin, receive grace, grow in holiness, and follow Jesus faithfully in ordinary life.
If you have been following Gospel Warrior, invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who are unsure what they believe to join us.
And there is something more personal I want to share with those who believe this ministry is worth sustaining.
Gospel Warrior cannot fulfill its mission merely by publishing another moving article.
The goal is deeper than a moment of emotion on a screen.
We want people to open their Bibles.
To understand what they read.
To grow in prayer.
To confront destructive patterns.
To discover sound Christian resources.
To learn what it means to follow Jesus when nobody is watching.
These resources are intended to help make biblical nourishment and spiritual growth accessible, including to people who may not have the means to purchase Christian books and study materials.
And keeping a ministry like this going requires real support.
Time.
Research.
Writing.
Resource development.
Ongoing maintenance.
The work of making Christian teaching and discipleship materials available to more people.
Not because God measures your devotion by a recurring payment.
And certainly not because anyone can purchase forgiveness, blessing, or spiritual standing through financial support.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not something bought with money. Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And in Philippians 4:15–18, he acknowledged the generosity of believers who supported his ministry.
That gives us a beautiful biblical way to understand voluntary support.
We respect those convictions.
It is an opportunity to participate willingly in work you believe is helping people encounter biblical truth.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Grow.
The Gospel is not behind a payment wall.
Our invitation is simply this: if you have the means, believe in this mission, and want to help sustain and expand it, consider standing with us as a monthly supporter.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
A thoughtful comment can open a conversation.
And a prayer for this ministry is never something we should treat lightly.
We do not want supporters who feel pressured by guilt.
We want people who understand the mission, believe it is worth supporting, and give freely as the Lord leads them.
Because the Gospel we preach is not for sale.
And the Jesus we proclaim does not need financial transactions to make His grace available.
He has already paid the price of redemption through His own blood.
Which brings us to one final question.
What will you do with the truth John has placed before you?
Will you continue explaining away what God is calling you to confess?
Will you keep rehearsing the failures of others while refusing to examine your own heart?
Will you use the language of grace to excuse a sin you have no intention of surrendering?
Or will you come honestly to the One who is faithful and just to forgive?
Perhaps tonight you need to put down your phone and pray.
Perhaps you need to open your Bible to 1 John and read slowly.
Perhaps you need to apologize to someone.
Perhaps you need to seek help for a destructive habit.
Perhaps you need to tell a trusted, mature Christian that you are struggling and need accountability.
Perhaps you need to stop hiding behind the appearance of being spiritually strong.
Or perhaps, after years of believing you have gone too far, you simply need to hear again that Jesus Christ is the righteous Advocate John proclaims.
Whatever your situation, do not leave this passage merely impressed by its beauty.
Let its truth bring you before Christ.
Because 1 John 1:9 was never meant to make us comfortable with sin.
It was written to assure those who confess their sins of God's faithfulness and forgiveness.
And the warnings surrounding it are not there to rob repentant sinners of hope.
They are there to expose the deadly illusion that we can have truth while refusing to acknowledge our need for mercy.
The warning is serious.
But the invitation is glorious.
There is cleansing through the blood of Jesus.
There is forgiveness grounded in His saving work.
There is an Advocate with the Father.
There is grace for sinners who come into the light.
And there is a Savior whose power to redeem is greater than the darkness we once tried so desperately to conceal.
So come into the light.
Not because you have become flawless.
But because Jesus is faithful.
Not because your history is clean.
But because His blood cleanses from sin.
Not because your story has never contained scandal.
But because in Christ, scandal does not have to be the ending.
The sin you are terrified to bring into the light is already known to Jesus—and the Savior who knows the whole truth is still calling you to come to Him.
